title: Custody death an accident: jury
article: Victoria Police Department should tighten its jail policies and increase first aid training, a coroner's jury looking into a death in police cells last year has recommended.
The jury, which made 12 recommendations yesterday, concluded the death of 48-year-old Kevin John Vigar was accidental.
Vigar died of alcohol poisoning June 27, 2009, after being picked up for public intoxication. He was later found to have a blood-alcohol content of .498, more than six times the legal driving limit.

When Vigar and two friends were picked up by police after being spotted passed out on a sidewalk, they were responsive, and were led to a police van without a full medical assessment, although ambulance paramedics were at the scene.

In his summation to the jury, presiding coroner Shane DeMeyer said a formal protocol for police and paramedics in such situations did not seem to be in place, and there appeared to be no clear idea of who would take the lead.

The jury recommended that there be visible postings in Victoria police cells of all medical care policies, including "rousability and questionable consciousness," and that a prisoner medical information sheet should be reviewed and updated.

It said all jail officers should have level three first-aid certification and the department should ensure current first-aid training for all staff, with mandatory recertification training. Also, Victoria police department jail guards should have training equivalent to those in Vancouver, the jury recommended.

B.C. Ambulance Service should do a mandatory, documented physical assessment at the scene and a copy of the patient care report should accompany those taken into custody, said the jury, which also called for more detox and sobering beds.
Coroner's counsel Rod MacKenzie said he was pleased with the recommendations.

"The jury has come up with some things that may well assist with the difficult business of assessing prisoners who are brought in intoxicated," he said. "I believe communication between police and ambulance [staff] is vital and that is reflected in one of the jury's recommendations."
Richard Vigar, Kevin's half-brother, told the inquest yesterday that Kevin began drinking at 15 or 16, and had a father with alcohol problems.
"He made it to Grade 10, and after that he was in and out of jobs," said Richard, one of 23 witnesses called during the three days of proceedings.
Richard said he saw his brother regularly, and about half the time Kevin would show up drunk. Still, he said, Kevin kept himself clean and was "a very outgoing, happy guy."
He said the family knew Kevin's life was threatened by his drinking.
"It was kind of like a cat having nine lives. We really didn't think he was going to last as long as he did."

Clinical social worker Bob McKechnie told the inquest yesterday that Vigar had been at the Vancouver Island Health Authority's Sobering and Assessment Centre just eight days before his death. He was also there twice last year and multiple times from 2004 to 2007.
The centre, which offers short-term shelter and evaluation for up to 20 people, operates at near-capacity with 7,000 clients a year.
